text: Lesson 13 built a tag-checking script around az. This lesson writes the direct AWS equivalent — the same bash, the same command-substitution-and-loop pattern, pointed at EC2 instances instead of resource groups, to list every instance in a region along with its running state and who owns it.

aws ec2 describe-instances returns every instance, but one level deeper than az group list: AWS nests instances inside reservations, so the query walks Reservations, then Instances, then InstanceId before it reaches a usable value. --output text is AWS's version of -o tsv — plain lines, one instance ID per line, exactly the shape a for loop wants.

Nothing about bash itself changes crossing from az to aws. Command substitution still captures output as a value the same way. The query language is the same JMESPath az used, just aimed at a differently nested response shape. --output text plays the same role -o tsv played before it — flattening JSON down into lines a loop can consume one at a time.

Inside the loop, --instance-ids narrows the describe call to one instance, pulling its State.Name and an Owner tag with a filter: Tags where Key equals Owner, take the Value, then the first match with [0]. The real catch to remember: AWS text output prints the literal word None for a missing value, not an empty line the way az's tsv output did — so the check matches that exact string instead of using bash's -z test.

The complete script, check-ec2-owners.sh, lists every instance ID, loops over them, pulls the state and owner tag for each one, and reports OK with the owner name or MISSING TAG when there isn't one. Structurally it's identical to Lesson 13's check-tags.sh — list, loop, check, report — because that shape was never actually specific to Azure in the first place.

Running check-ec2-owners.sh produces the same kind of flat, scannable report Lesson 13 produced, just for EC2 instances and their states instead of resource groups and tags. Next up: jq, a tool built specifically to make pulling fields like these out of JSON far less fragile than leaning on --query and text parsing alone.
